statement: Every proper [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ with $1$ lies in a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) of $R$.

hypotheses.text: $R$ is a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) with $1$.
$I$ is an [ideal](c:ideal) of $R$ with $I \neq R$.

conclusion: There is a maximal ideal $M$ of $R$ with $I \subseteq M$.

proofs.name: Zorn's lemma
proofs.slogan: Order the proper ideals above $I$ by inclusion and take a maximal one by Zorn's lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The same proof works for one-sided ideals of a noncommutative ring with $1$.

roles.why: The element $1$ turns 'proper' into '$1$ is not in the ideal', which survives unions.
The ideal $I$ is a member of the family, so the family is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Collect the proper ideals that contain $I$ into a family $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of ideals $J$ with $I \subseteq J \neq R$, ordered by inclusion. This is a [partial order](c:partial-order). It contains $I$, so $\mathcal P$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Show that every nonempty [chain](c:chain) in $\mathcal P$ has an upper bound in $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal C$ be a nonempty chain and $U = \bigcup \mathcal C$. Two elements of $U$ lie in one member of $\mathcal C$, so $U$ is closed under sums and under multiples by $R$. Every member omits $1$, so $1 \notin U$, and $U \in \mathcal P$ bounds $\mathcal C$.

steps.slogan: Extract a maximal element $M$ of $\mathcal P$ by Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: The set $\mathcal P$ is nonempty and every chain has an upper bound. Zorn's lemma gives a member $M$ of $\mathcal P$ with no member of $\mathcal P$ strictly above it.

steps.slogan: Show that $M$ is a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) of $R$ that contains $I$.
steps.detail: The ideal $M$ is proper and $I \subseteq M$. Let $J$ be an ideal with $M \subsetneq J$. Then $I \subseteq J$, and $J \notin \mathcal P$ by the choice of $M$, so $J = R$.

concepts.c:ideal: The theorem concerns ideals, and the family consists of ideals.
concepts.c:commutative-ring: The ring supplies the ideals and the element $1$.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: The maximal element of the family is the ideal that the theorem asks for.
concepts.c:partial-order: Inclusion orders the family, as Zorn's lemma needs.
concepts.c:chain: A union of a chain is the candidate upper bound.

source.note: Krull's argument; see Atiyah and Macdonald, Introduction to Commutative Algebra, Chapter 1 (Theorem 1.3 and its corollary).

statement: Let $V$ and $W$ be real [normed spaces](c:normed-space). Every surjective [isometry](c:isometry) $f\colon V \to W$ is an [affine map](c:affine-map).

hypotheses.text: $V$ and $W$ are [normed spaces](c:normed-space) over $\mathbb{R}$.
The map $f$ is an [isometry](c:isometry): $\|f(x) - f(y)\| = \|x - y\|$ for all $x, y \in V$.
The map $f$ is surjective.

conclusion: There are a linear map $T\colon V \to W$ and a vector $w \in W$ with $f(x) = Tx + w$ for all $x \in V$.

proofs.name: Metric midpoints
proofs.slogan: Describe the midpoint of two points by distances alone, so $f$ keeps midpoints, and a midpoint-preserving continuous map is affine.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for $V$ and $W$ of any dimension, with no strict convexity. The case $a = b$ is trivial.

roles.why: The vector structure gives the midpoint $z = (a+b)/2$ and the reflection $x \mapsto a + b - x$, an isometry of $V$.
Distances are kept, so a set defined by distances maps to the matching set; continuity follows.
A surjection turns 'for all $y$ in $A_n$' into the same statement in $W$.

steps.slogan: Define sets $A_n$ of metric [midpoints](c:midpoint) of $a$ and $b$ from distances alone.
steps.detail: Let $A_0 = \{x : \|x - a\| = \|x - b\| = \tfrac12 \|a - b\|\}$. Let $A_{n+1}$ be the set of $x \in A_n$ with $\|x - y\| \le \tfrac12 \operatorname{diam} A_n$ for all $y \in A_n$. The set $A_0$ is bounded, since it lies in the ball of radius $\tfrac12\|a-b\|$ around $a$.

steps.slogan: Show that the sets $A_n$ shrink to the single point $z = (a+b)/2$.
steps.detail: The reflection $\sigma(x) = a + b - x$ is an isometry that fixes $z$ and maps each $A_n$ onto itself, by induction. For $y \in A_n$ we get $\|y - z\| = \tfrac12 \|y - \sigma y\| \le \tfrac12 \operatorname{diam} A_n$, so $z \in A_n$ for all $n$. By definition $\operatorname{diam} A_{n+1} \le \tfrac12 \operatorname{diam} A_n$, so $\bigcap_n A_n = \{z\}$.

steps.slogan: Carry the construction through $f$ to show that $f$ keeps midpoints.
steps.detail: A surjective isometry is a bijection that keeps distances and diameters. By induction, $f(A_n)$ is the set built from $f(a), f(b)$ in $W$. Step 2 in $W$ then gives $f(z) = \tfrac12 (f(a) + f(b))$.

steps.slogan: Subtract $f(0)$ to get $g$ with $g(0) = 0$, and show that $g$ is additive.
steps.detail: The map $g = f - f(0)$ is a surjective isometry that keeps midpoints. The point $x/2$ is the midpoint of $0$ and $x$, so $g(x/2) = g(x)/2$. Then $g(x + y)/2 = g((x+y)/2) = (g(x) + g(y))/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that the additive continuous map $g$ is real linear, so $f = g + f(0)$ is affine.
steps.detail: An additive map satisfies $g(qx) = q\,g(x)$ for every rational $q$. The isometry $g$ is continuous, so approximating a real $t$ by rationals gives $g(tx) = t\,g(x)$. So $g$ is linear and $f$ is [affine](c:affine-map).

concepts.c:normed-space: The norm defines the distances that describe the midpoint.
concepts.c:isometry: The map keeps distances, so it keeps distance-defined sets.
concepts.c:affine-map: The proof ends by showing that $f$ is a translate of a linear map.
concepts.c:midpoint: The midpoint is the only point left in the shrinking sets.

source.note: J. Väisälä, A proof of the Mazur-Ulam theorem, American Mathematical Monthly 110 (2003), 633-635.

statement: Let $\mathcal G$ be an [algebra of sets](c:algebra-of-sets) on $\Omega$. The smallest monotone class that contains $\mathcal G$ equals the [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\sigma(\mathcal G)$. A monotone class is closed under unions of increasing sequences and intersections of decreasing sequences.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal G$ is an [algebra of sets](c:algebra-of-sets) on $\Omega$: it contains $\Omega$ and is closed under complements and finite unions.

conclusion: The smallest monotone class $m(\mathcal G)$ containing $\mathcal G$ equals $\sigma(\mathcal G)$.

proofs.name: Good sets
proofs.slogan: Show that the monotone class generated by the algebra is closed under intersections and differences, so it is a sigma-algebra.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for an algebra on any set $\Omega$. The inclusion $m(\mathcal G) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal G)$ is easy, and the work is the other inclusion.

roles.why: The algebra puts $\mathcal G$ inside each good class and gives $\Omega \in \mathcal M$ for complements.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathcal M = m(\mathcal G)$ lies in $\sigma(\mathcal G)$.
steps.detail: A [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) is closed under countable unions and intersections, so it is a monotone class. So $\sigma(\mathcal G)$ is a monotone class that contains $\mathcal G$, and $\mathcal M$ is the smallest such class.

steps.slogan: Define the good class $\mathcal M_A$ of sets that combine well with $A \in \mathcal M$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal M_A = \{B : A \cap B,\ A \setminus B,\ B \setminus A \in \mathcal M\}$. If $B_n$ is monotone with limit $B$, the three sequences with $A$ are monotone with limits in $\mathcal M$. So $\mathcal M_A$ is a monotone class, and $B \in \mathcal M_A$ iff $A \in \mathcal M_B$.

steps.slogan: Bootstrap twice to close $\mathcal M$ under intersections and differences.
steps.detail: For $A \in \mathcal G$ the algebra gives $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal M_A$, so $\mathcal M \subseteq \mathcal M_A$. By symmetry, $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal M_B$ for each $B \in \mathcal M$, so $\mathcal M \subseteq \mathcal M_B$. Hence $A \cap B$ and $A \setminus B$ lie in $\mathcal M$ for all $A, B \in \mathcal M$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathcal M$ is an algebra of sets.
steps.detail: The set $\Omega$ lies in $\mathcal G \subseteq \mathcal M$, so $A^c = \Omega \setminus A \in \mathcal M$ for $A \in \mathcal M$. Then $A \cup B = (A^c \cap B^c)^c \in \mathcal M$. So $\mathcal M$ is closed under complements and finite unions.

steps.slogan: Show that an algebra that is a monotone class is a sigma-algebra, and conclude.
steps.detail: For $A_1, A_2, \dots \in \mathcal M$ the finite unions $B_n = A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_n$ lie in $\mathcal M$ and increase to $\bigcup A_n$, which lies in $\mathcal M$. So $\mathcal M$ is a sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal G$, hence $\sigma(\mathcal G) \subseteq \mathcal M$. With step 1, $\mathcal M = \sigma(\mathcal G)$.

concepts.c:algebra-of-sets: The generating family is an algebra, and the proof shows that $\mathcal M$ is one.
concepts.c:sigma-algebra: The goal is to show that $\mathcal M$ is the generated sigma-algebra.

source.note: P. R. Halmos, Measure Theory, section on monotone classes.

statement: Let $R$ be a [well-founded](c:well-founded-relation) [extensional](c:extensional-relation) relation on a set $E$. Then there is a unique [transitive set](c:transitive-set) $T$ and a unique isomorphism $\pi\colon (E, R) \to (T, \in)$.

hypotheses.text: $R$ is [well-founded](c:well-founded-relation) on $E$: every nonempty subset has an $R$-minimal element.
$R$ is [extensional](c:extensional-relation): elements with the same $R$-predecessors are equal.

conclusion: There is exactly one pair $(T, \pi)$ with $T$ transitive and $\pi$ an isomorphism from $(E, R)$ onto $(T, \in)$.

proofs.name: Collapse by recursion
proofs.slogan: Define $\pi(x) = \{\pi(y) : y\,R\,x\}$ by well-founded recursion and check that it is an isomorphism onto a transitive set.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem in ZF without choice. Replacement defines $\pi$ and makes its image a set.

roles.why: Well-foundedness allows recursion and induction along $R$.
Extensionality turns equal predecessor images into equal elements.

steps.slogan: Define $\pi$ on $E$ by [well-founded recursion](c:well-founded-induction) along $R$.
steps.detail: Set $\pi(x) = \{\pi(y) : y\,R\,x\}$. The recursion theorem for well-founded relations gives one such function, and the [axiom of replacement](c:axiom-of-replacement) makes each $\pi(x)$ and the image $T = \pi[E]$ sets.

steps.slogan: Show that the image $T = \pi[E]$ is a [transitive set](c:transitive-set).
steps.detail: If $u \in \pi(x)$ with $x \in E$, then $u = \pi(y)$ for some $y\,R\,x$, so $u \in T$. Hence each element of $T$ is a subset of $T$.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction along $R$ that $\pi$ is injective, using extensionality.
steps.detail: Assume that $\pi(y) = \pi(y')$ implies $y = y'$ for every $y\,R\,x$. Let $\pi(x) = \pi(x')$. A predecessor $y$ of $x$ has $\pi(y) \in \pi(x')$, so $\pi(y) = \pi(z)$ with $z\,R\,x'$, and $y = z$. The same argument runs back. So $x, x'$ have the same predecessors, and $x = x'$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\pi$ keeps and reflects the relation, so it is an isomorphism onto $T$.
steps.detail: If $x\,R\,y$, then $\pi(x) \in \pi(y)$ by definition. If $\pi(x) \in \pi(y)$, then $\pi(x) = \pi(z)$ for some $z\,R\,y$, so $x = z$ by injectivity and $x\,R\,y$.

steps.slogan: Show that every isomorphism onto a transitive set equals $\pi$, so $T$ and $\pi$ are unique.
steps.detail: Let $\sigma\colon (E, R) \to (T', \in)$ be an isomorphism with $T'$ transitive. An element of $\sigma(x)$ lies in $T'$ by transitivity, so it is $\sigma(y)$ with $y\,R\,x$. So $\sigma(x) = \{\sigma(y) : y\,R\,x\}$, the recursion of $\pi$. Induction along $R$ gives $\sigma = \pi$ and $T' = T$.

concepts.c:well-founded-relation: It gives the minimal elements that make recursion and induction along $R$ work.
concepts.c:transitive-set: The image of the collapse must be transitive, and transitivity forces uniqueness.
concepts.c:well-founded-induction: Both the definition of $\pi$ and the proofs about it run along $R$.
concepts.c:axiom-of-replacement: It turns the recursion into a function whose image is a set.

source.note: A. Mostowski (1949); see T. Jech, Set Theory (3rd ed.), the collapsing theorem for well-founded relations.

statement: Every [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ of a [free group](c:free-group) $F$ is free. If $F$ has finite rank $k$ and $H$ has finite index $n$, then $H$ is free of rank $nk - n + 1$.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is a [free group](c:free-group).
$H$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $F$.
For the rank formula, $F$ has finite rank $k$ and $H$ has finite index $n$.

conclusion: The group $H$ is free, and its rank is $nk - n + 1$ when $k$ and $n$ are finite.

proofs.name: Covering graph
proofs.slogan: Realize $F$ as the fundamental group of a graph, take the covering graph that belongs to $H$, and read a free basis off a spanning tree.
proofs.scope: Free groups of any rank; a spanning tree of an infinite graph uses Zorn's lemma. If $k = 0$, then $F$ and $H$ are trivial and free of rank $0$.

roles.why: A free group is the fundamental group of a wedge of circles.
Covering space theory attaches a covering space to $H$.
Finite rank and index make the covering graph finite, so its edges can be counted.

steps.slogan: Realize $F$ as the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) of a wedge of circles $X$.
steps.detail: Take one circle for each free generator and join them at one point to get a [wedge sum](c:wedge-sum) $X$. It is a connected graph with one vertex and $k$ edges. By the Seifert-van Kampen theorem, $\pi_1(X)$ is free on the loops of the circles, so $\pi_1(X) \cong F$.

steps.slogan: Take the [covering space](c:covering-space) $p\colon \tilde X \to X$ that belongs to $H$.
steps.detail: A graph is locally path connected and semilocally simply connected, so the classification of covering spaces gives a connected cover $\tilde X$ with $p_*\pi_1(\tilde X) = H$. The map $p_*$ is injective, so $\pi_1(\tilde X) \cong H$. The number of sheets is the index $[F : H]$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\tilde X$ is a connected graph.
steps.detail: The preimage of the vertex is a discrete set. Each open edge is evenly covered, so its preimage is a disjoint union of open arcs. These lifted vertices and edges make $\tilde X$ a graph.

steps.slogan: Collapse a spanning tree $T$ of $\tilde X$ to show that $\pi_1(\tilde X)$ is free.
steps.detail: A connected graph has a [spanning tree](c:spanning-tree) $T$, and $T$ is contractible. So $\tilde X \simeq \tilde X / T$, a wedge of circles with one circle for each edge outside $T$. Hence $H \cong \pi_1(\tilde X)$ is free on the edges outside $T$.

steps.slogan: Count the vertices and edges of $\tilde X$ to read off the rank $nk - n + 1$.
steps.detail: Each of the $n$ sheets contains a lift of the vertex and of each of the $k$ edges, so $\tilde X$ has $n$ vertices and $nk$ edges. The tree $T$ has $n - 1$ edges, so $nk - (n-1)$ edges lie outside $T$.

concepts.c:free-group: The free group is both the group $F$ and the group $H$ that we obtain.
concepts.c:subgroup: The subgroup $H$ selects the covering space.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: It links groups to graphs: $F$ and $H$ are fundamental groups of graphs.
concepts.c:wedge-sum: The wedge of circles is the graph with fundamental group $F$.
concepts.c:covering-space: The cover of the wedge has fundamental group $H$.
concepts.c:spanning-tree: Its complement of edges gives a free basis.

source.note: A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, section 1.A on graphs and free groups.

statement: Let a two-terminal DC network of [linear](c:linear-circuit) resistors and independent sources have exactly one state for each terminal voltage. Then at its terminals it acts like a current source $I_N$ in parallel with a resistor $R_N$. Here $I_N$ is the short-circuit current and $R_N$ is the resistance seen with all sources turned off.

hypotheses.text: The network has two terminals and contains only [linear](c:linear-circuit) resistors and independent DC sources.
For every voltage $V$ applied at the terminals, the network has exactly one state.

conclusion: The terminal current obeys $I = I_N - V/R_N$ for every terminal voltage $V$, the law of a current source $I_N$ in parallel with $R_N$.

new_concepts.name: linear circuit
new_concepts.reminder: A circuit whose element laws are linear, so its equations are linear in the sources.
new_concepts.definition: A circuit of resistors and independent sources whose Ohm and Kirchhoff equations are linear in the voltages and currents.

proofs.name: Superposition
proofs.slogan: Split the terminal current into a part from the internal sources and a part from the terminal voltage, using linearity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem in DC steady state. If $R_N = \infty$, the network acts as a pure current source; only the terminal law is claimed to match.

roles.why: Linear elements give linear equations, and resistors dissipate power, which fixes the sign of $1/R_N$.
A unique solution for each $V$ lets superposition split the solution into two parts.

steps.slogan: Drive the terminals with a voltage $V$ and name the current out of terminal A as $I(V)$.
steps.detail: Kirchhoff's laws and Ohm's law form a [system of linear equations](c:system-of-linear-equations) in the node voltages and branch currents. The independent sources and $V$ are its inputs. By hypothesis it has one solution for each $V$, so $I(V)$ is a well-defined function.

steps.slogan: Split $I(V)$ by [superposition](c:superposition) into a source part and a voltage part.
steps.detail: The system is linear with a unique solution, so the solution is the sum of the one with $V = 0$ and the one with all independent sources off and terminal voltage $V$. So $I(V) = I(0) + I_{\mathrm{off}}(V)$. Here $I(0)$ is the short-circuit current $I_N$.

steps.slogan: Show that the source-off current equals $-V/R_N$ for a constant $R_N$.
steps.detail: The source-off solution depends linearly on $V$, so $I_{\mathrm{off}}(V) = -G_N V$ for a constant $G_N$. The resistors absorb power $-V I_{\mathrm{off}} = G_N V^2 \ge 0$, so $G_N \ge 0$. The resistance seen from the terminals is $R_N = 1/G_N$.

steps.slogan: Compare the network law with the law of a current source $I_N$ in parallel with $R_N$.
steps.detail: In that circuit, the current out of terminal A is $I_N$ minus the current $V/R_N$ in the resistor, so $I = I_N - V/R_N$, the same law. An outside circuit meets the network only through $(V, I)$, so its voltages and currents stay the same when the network is replaced.

concepts.c:linear-circuit: Linearity of the elements is what makes superposition valid.
concepts.c:system-of-linear-equations: The circuit laws form a linear system whose unique solution gives $I(V)$.
concepts.c:superposition: It splits the response into the source part and the voltage part.

source.note: Standard derivation by superposition; see Alexander and Sadiku, Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, section on Norton's theorem.

statement: A [plane wave](c:plane-wave) $e^{ikz}$ meets a scatterer, and the scattered wave is $f(\theta, \varphi)\,e^{ikr}/r$ for large $r$, with $f$ smooth near $\theta = 0$. If probability is conserved, then $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{el}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{abs}} = \frac{4\pi}{k} \operatorname{Im} f(0)$, where $\sigma_{\mathrm{el}} = \int |f|^2\, d\Omega$.

hypotheses.text: The stationary state is $\psi \sim e^{ikz} + f(\theta, \varphi)\, e^{ikr}/r$ as $r \to \infty$, with $f$ continuous at $\theta = 0$.
Probability is conserved ([unitarity](c:unitarity)): the net outward flux through a large sphere equals minus the rate at which the scatterer absorbs probability.

conclusion: The total cross section satisfies $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}} = \frac{4\pi}{k} \operatorname{Im} f(0)$.

new_concepts.name: scattering amplitude
new_concepts.reminder: The coefficient $f$ of the outgoing spherical wave $e^{ikr}/r$ in the scattered wave.
new_concepts.definition: For a scattering state $\psi \sim e^{ikz} + f(\theta, \varphi)\, e^{ikr}/r$, the function $f$ is the scattering amplitude; $|f|^2$ is the differential cross section.

proofs.name: Flux balance
proofs.slogan: Balance the probability flux through a large sphere, and find the forward amplitude in the interference of the incident and scattered waves.
proofs.scope: Nonrelativistic scattering at wave number $k$ with absorption allowed. This is the standard physics derivation; the [stationary phase](c:stationary-phase) step is done to leading order in $1/r$.

roles.why: The asymptotic form of $\psi$ gives the three parts of the current and their flux.
It sets the total flux through the sphere equal to minus the absorption rate.

steps.slogan: Write the probability current of the asymptotic state as three parts: incident, scattered and interference.
steps.detail: With $\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{in}} + \psi_{\mathrm{sc}}$ the current $\mathbf j = \frac{\hbar}{m} \operatorname{Im}(\psi^* \nabla \psi)$ splits into $\mathbf j_{\mathrm{in}} + \mathbf j_{\mathrm{sc}} + \mathbf j_{\mathrm{int}}$, the last being the cross term. The incident flux density is $v = \hbar k/m$.

steps.slogan: Equate the net outward flux through a large sphere to minus the absorption rate.
steps.detail: By [unitarity](c:unitarity), the flux $\oint \mathbf j \cdot d\mathbf S$ through a sphere of radius $r$ equals $-v\,\sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}$, minus the rate at which the scatterer absorbs probability.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the incident flux and the scattered flux.
steps.detail: A plane wave has zero net flux through a closed surface. For the scattered wave $\mathbf j_{\mathrm{sc}} \approx v |f|^2 \hat r / r^2$, so its flux tends to $v \int |f|^2\, d\Omega = v\,\sigma_{\mathrm{el}}$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the interference flux by [stationary phase](c:stationary-phase) at the forward direction.
steps.detail: The cross term gives flux $v\, r \int (1 + \cos\theta) \operatorname{Re}\big[f\, e^{ikr(1 - \cos\theta)}\big] d\Omega$. For large $r$ only the end $\theta = 0$ contributes, and the flux tends to $-v\,\frac{4\pi}{k} \operatorname{Im} f(0)$.

steps.slogan: Add the three fluxes and solve for the total cross section.
steps.detail: The balance gives $v\,\sigma_{\mathrm{el}} - v\,\frac{4\pi}{k} \operatorname{Im} f(0) = -v\,\sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}$. Hence $\frac{4\pi}{k} \operatorname{Im} f(0) = \sigma_{\mathrm{el}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{abs}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}$.

concepts.c:plane-wave: The incident wave is a plane wave, which interferes with the scattered wave.
concepts.c:unitarity: Conservation of probability links the flux through the sphere to absorption.
concepts.c:stationary-phase: It shows that the interference flux comes from the forward direction only.

source.note: Standard flux-balance derivation in scattering texts, for example J. J. Sakurai, Modern Quantum Mechanics, and R. G. Newton, Scattering Theory of Waves and Particles.

statement: Let a rigid body of mass $m$ have its [center of mass](c:barycenter) on an axis $\ell_C$, and let $\ell$ be an axis parallel to $\ell_C$ at distance $d$. Then $I_\ell = I_C + m d^2$, where $I$ is the [moment of inertia](c:moment-of-inertia) about the axis.

hypotheses.text: The body is a mass distribution $\mu$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with finite total mass $m$ and finite moments of inertia.
The axis $\ell_C$ passes through the [center of mass](c:barycenter) of the body.
The axis $\ell$ is parallel to $\ell_C$ and at distance $d$ from it.

conclusion: The moments of inertia satisfy $I_\ell = I_C + m d^2$.

new_concepts.name: moment of inertia
new_concepts.reminder: The integral of mass times squared distance to an axis, which measures resistance to rotation.
new_concepts.definition: For a mass distribution $\mu$ and an axis $\ell$, the moment of inertia is $I_\ell = \int \operatorname{dist}(\mathbf r, \ell)^2\, d\mu(\mathbf r)$.

proofs.name: Expand the squared distance
proofs.slogan: Shift the axis by a vector $\mathbf d$, expand the squared distance, and cancel the cross term with the definition of the center of mass.
proofs.scope: Any axis direction and any finite mass distribution. The case $d = 0$ is trivial.

roles.why: Finite mass and moments make every integral in the expansion finite.
With the center of mass at the origin, the first moment $\int \mathbf r\, d\mu$ is zero.
Parallel axes differ by a shift $\mathbf d$ in the plane perpendicular to them.

steps.slogan: Put the origin at the [center of mass](c:barycenter) and measure distances in the plane perpendicular to the axes.
steps.detail: Let $\mathbf u$ be the unit direction of both axes and $P\mathbf r = \mathbf r - (\mathbf r \cdot \mathbf u)\mathbf u$ the projection onto the plane orthogonal to $\mathbf u$. The axis $\ell_C$ passes through $0$, and $\ell$ meets the plane at a point $\mathbf d$ with $|\mathbf d| = d$. A point $\mathbf r$ has distance $|P\mathbf r|$ from $\ell_C$ and $|P\mathbf r - \mathbf d|$ from $\ell$.

steps.slogan: Expand the squared distance to $\ell$ into three terms.
steps.detail: Then $I_\ell = \int |P\mathbf r - \mathbf d|^2 d\mu = \int |P\mathbf r|^2 d\mu - 2\,\mathbf d \cdot \int P\mathbf r\, d\mu + d^2 \int d\mu$. The first term is $I_C$ and the last term is $m d^2$.

steps.slogan: Show that the cross term is zero because the origin is the center of mass.
steps.detail: The center of mass at the origin means $\int \mathbf r\, d\mu = 0$. The projection $P$ is linear, so $\int P\mathbf r\, d\mu = P \int \mathbf r\, d\mu = 0$. So the middle term vanishes.

steps.slogan: Add the remaining terms to obtain $I_\ell = I_C + m d^2$.
steps.detail: With the cross term gone, $I_\ell = \int |P\mathbf r|^2 d\mu + d^2 m$. The first integral is the [moment of inertia](c:moment-of-inertia) $I_C$.

concepts.c:barycenter: Its defining property $\int \mathbf r\, d\mu = 0$ kills the cross term.
concepts.c:moment-of-inertia: The theorem relates the moments of inertia about two parallel axes.

source.note: Standard proof; see Goldstein, Poole and Safko, Classical Mechanics, in the chapter on rigid body kinematics.

statement: In a real or complex [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) with [norm](c:norm) $\|x\| = \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle}$, all vectors $x, y$ satisfy $\|x + y\|^2 + \|x - y\|^2 = 2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2$.

hypotheses.text: $V$ is a real or complex [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) with the [norm](c:norm) $\|x\| = \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle}$.

proofs.name: Expand the inner products
proofs.slogan: Expand both squared norms with the inner product and let the cross terms cancel.
proofs.scope: Real and complex spaces. The converse, that a norm with this identity comes from an inner product, is the separate Jordan-von Neumann theorem.

roles.why: The inner product is additive in each slot, and the norm squared is $\langle x, x\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\|x + y\|^2$ by additivity of the inner product in each slot.
steps.detail: We get $\|x+y\|^2 = \langle x, x\rangle + \langle x, y\rangle + \langle y, x\rangle + \langle y, y\rangle$. In a complex space $\langle y, x\rangle = \overline{\langle x, y\rangle}$, so the middle terms add to $2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y\rangle$. So $\|x+y\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y\rangle + \|y\|^2$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\|x - y\|^2$ in the same way.
steps.detail: Replace $y$ by $-y$. Since $\langle x, -y\rangle = -\langle x, y\rangle$ and $\|-y\| = \|y\|$, we get $\|x-y\|^2 = \|x\|^2 - 2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y\rangle + \|y\|^2$.

steps.slogan: Add the two expansions so that the cross terms cancel.
steps.detail: The terms $2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y\rangle$ and $-2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y\rangle$ cancel. What remains is $2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2$.

concepts.c:inner-product-space: Its inner product is the source of the expansions.
concepts.c:norm: The norm squared is the inner product of a vector with itself.

source.note: Textbook computation; see Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, section on norms (the parallelogram equality).

statement: Let $f$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $R = [t_0 - a, t_0 + a] \times \overline B(y_0, b) \subset \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $M = \max_R |f|$. The [initial value problem](c:initial-value-problem) $y' = f(t, y)$, $y(t_0) = y_0$ has a solution on $[t_0 - h, t_0 + h]$, where $h = \min(a, b/M)$, and $h = a$ if $M = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is defined on the compact rectangle $R$, with $a, b > 0$.
The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $R$.

conclusion: A $C^1$ function $y\colon [t_0 - h, t_0 + h] \to \overline B(y_0, b)$ has $y' = f(t, y)$ and $y(t_0) = y_0$.

proofs.name: Euler polygons and compactness
proofs.slogan: Build Euler polygons with shrinking steps, extract a uniformly convergent subsequence, and show that the limit solves the integral equation.
proofs.scope: Forward time $t \ge t_0$; the backward interval follows by applying the result to $s \mapsto y(t_0 - s)$. If $M = 0$, the constant function $y_0$ is a solution.

roles.why: Compactness of $R$ gives the bound $M$ and the uniform continuity of $f$.
Continuity makes the slopes of the polygons defined, bounded and close to $f$ along the path.

steps.slogan: Build the Euler polygon $y_N$ with $N$ equal steps on $[t_0, t_0 + h]$ inside $R$.
steps.detail: Let $t_k = t_0 + kh/N$, $y_N(t_0) = y_0$ and $y_N(t) = y_N(t_k) + f(t_k, y_N(t_k))(t - t_k)$ on $[t_k, t_{k+1}]$. While the polygon is in $R$, its slopes have norm at most $M$, so $|y_N(t) - y_0| \le M h \le b$. Induction on $k$ shows that $y_N$ exists on the whole interval.

steps.slogan: Show that the polygons are uniformly bounded and $M$-[Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function).
steps.detail: Every $y_N$ stays in $\overline B(y_0, b)$ and has slopes of norm at most $M$. So $|y_N(t) - y_N(s)| \le M|t - s|$, and the family is bounded and [equicontinuous](c:equicontinuity).

steps.slogan: Extract a uniformly convergent subsequence $y_{N_j} \to y$ from the polygons.
steps.detail: The family is bounded and equicontinuous on a compact interval, so the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem gives a subsequence that converges uniformly to a continuous $y$. The limit has $y(t_0) = y_0$ and $|y(t) - y_0| \le b$.

steps.slogan: Show that each polygon solves the integral equation up to an error that tends to $0$.
steps.detail: On $(t_k, t_{k+1})$ we have $|t - t_k| \le h/N$ and $|y_N(t) - y_N(t_k)| \le Mh/N$. The function $f$ is [uniformly continuous](c:uniformly-continuous-map) on $R$, so $\varepsilon_N = \sup |y_N'(t) - f(t, y_N(t))| \to 0$. Hence $y_N(t) = y_0 + \int_{t_0}^t f(s, y_N(s))\, ds + e_N(t)$ with $|e_N| \le \varepsilon_N h$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit to get $y(t) = y_0 + \int_{t_0}^t f(s, y(s))\, ds$, then differentiate.
steps.detail: Uniform convergence and uniform continuity give $f(s, y_{N_j}(s)) \to f(s, y(s))$ uniformly, so the integrals converge, and $e_{N_j} \to 0$. This gives the integral equation. The integrand is continuous, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus $y$ is $C^1$ with $y' = f(t, y)$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $f$ drives the existence of the slopes and the limit.
concepts.c:initial-value-problem: The theorem gives a local solution of this problem.
concepts.c:lipschitz-function: The bound $M$ on the slopes makes every polygon Lipschitz.
concepts.c:equicontinuity: Equicontinuity of the polygons is what the compactness theorem needs.
concepts.c:uniformly-continuous-map: It makes the Euler error tend to $0$ uniformly.

source.note: Cauchy-Peano by Euler polygons and Ascoli's lemma; see Coddington and Levinson, Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations, Chapter 1.

statement: The number $\pi$ is [transcendental](c:transcendental-number): it is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients.
conclusion: The number $\pi$ is not an [algebraic number](c:algebraic-number).

proofs.name: From the Hermite-Lindemann theorem
proofs.slogan: If $\pi$ were algebraic, then $i\pi$ would be algebraic, and the Hermite-Lindemann theorem would make $e^{i\pi} = -1$ transcendental.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline that rests on the Hermite-Lindemann theorem, whose proof is the cited work. The argument is by contradiction.

steps.slogan: Assume that $\pi$ is algebraic, and aim for a contradiction.
steps.detail: Suppose that $\pi$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients. The next steps show that this contradicts the transcendence of $e^{i\pi}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $i\pi$ is a nonzero [algebraic number](c:algebraic-number).
steps.detail: The algebraic numbers form a field, and $i$ is algebraic as a root of $x^2 + 1$. So $i\pi$ is algebraic, and it is not $0$.

steps.slogan: Apply the Hermite-Lindemann theorem to $\alpha = i\pi$ to see that $e^{i\pi}$ is transcendental.
steps.detail: The cited work proves that $e^{\alpha}$ is [transcendental](c:transcendental-number) for every nonzero algebraic $\alpha$. For $\alpha = i\pi$ this makes $e^{i\pi}$ transcendental.

steps.slogan: Compare with Euler's identity $e^{i\pi} = -1$ to reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: Euler's formula gives $e^{i\pi} = \cos\pi + i\sin\pi = -1$. The number $-1$ is algebraic, as a root of $x + 1$, so it is not transcendental. This contradicts step 3, so $\pi$ is transcendental.

concepts.c:transcendental-number: The Hermite-Lindemann theorem makes $e^{i\pi}$ transcendental, and the claim is about $\pi$.
concepts.c:algebraic-number: The assumption that $\pi$ is algebraic leads to the contradiction.

source.ref: F. Lindemann, Ueber die Zahl pi, Mathematische Annalen 20 (1882), 213-225
source.note: Lindemann proves the transcendence of $e^{\alpha}$ for algebraic $\alpha \neq 0$ and derives that $\pi$ is transcendental from $e^{i\pi} = -1$.

statement: Let $G$ act on $\Omega$, let $f_i\colon H_i \to G$ be homomorphisms for at least two indices $i$, and let $X_i \subseteq \Omega$ be pairwise disjoint and nonempty with $f_i(h)X_j \subseteq X_i$ for $i \ne j$ and $h \ne 1$. If there are three indices or some $|H_i| \ge 3$, the induced map from the [free product](c:free-product) $\ast_i H_i$ to $G$ is injective.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ acts on a set $\Omega$, and the maps $f_i\colon H_i \to G$ are group homomorphisms for at least two indices $i$.
The sets $X_i \subseteq \Omega$ are nonempty and pairwise disjoint.
For $i \ne j$ and $h \in H_i$ with $h \ne 1$, we have $f_i(h)X_j \subseteq X_i$.
There are at least three indices, or some $H_i$ has at least three elements.

conclusion: The homomorphism $\ast_i H_i \to G$ induced by the $f_i$ is injective.

proofs.name: Reduced words move the sets
proofs.slogan: Show that every nonempty reduced word moves some ping-pong set into another one, so its image is not the identity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The cardinality hypothesis is used only when the first and last letters of a word leave no third index free.

roles.why: The action turns a word into a map of $\Omega$, and the identity fixes every $X_k$.
It sends each set $X_j$ into $X_i$ under a nontrivial letter of $H_i$.
Disjointness and nonemptiness make $X_k \subseteq X_i$ impossible for $k \ne i$.
It supplies a third index, or a factor with room for a conjugating letter.

steps.slogan: Write each element of the [free product](c:free-product) as a [reduced word](c:reduced-word).
steps.detail: Each element of $\ast_i H_i$ is a unique product $h_1 \cdots h_m$ with $h_r \in H_{i_r} \setminus \{1\}$ and $i_r \ne i_{r+1}$. The empty word is $1$. It suffices to show that every nonempty reduced word has image $\ne 1$, since then the kernel is trivial.

steps.slogan: Show by induction on length that a reduced word from $H_i$ to $H_j$ maps $X_k$ into $X_i$.
steps.detail: This holds for each $k \ne j$. For a single letter it is the ping-pong hypothesis. A longer word splits into reduced words $w_1 w_2$, where $w_1$ ends in a factor different from the first factor of $w_2$. Then $w_2 X_k \subseteq X_{\mathrm{first}(w_2)}$ and $w_1 X_{\mathrm{first}(w_2)} \subseteq X_i$ by induction.

steps.slogan: Treat a word whose first factor $i$ and last factor $j$ miss some index $k$.
steps.detail:
If the word $w$ had image $1$, then $X_k = w X_k \subseteq X_i$ by the previous step. But $X_k 
e \emptyset$ and $X_k \cap X_i = \emptyset$ since $k 
e i$, a contradiction. Such an index $k$ exists if there are three indices, or if $i = j$ (then any $k 
e i$ works).

steps.slogan: Treat the last case by conjugating with a letter from a factor with at least three elements.
steps.detail:
Now there are two indices, $i 
e j$, and some factor has three elements. Suppose it is $H_i$, else use $w^{-1}$. Pick $h \in H_i$ with $h 
e 1$ and $h h_1 
e 1$. The reduced word $h w h^{-1}$ starts and ends in $H_i$, so it has image $
e 1$ by the previous step, and so does $w$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the kernel of the induced map is trivial.
steps.detail: Every nonempty reduced word has image $\ne 1$ by steps 3 and 4. So only the empty word maps to $1$, and the homomorphism $\ast_i H_i \to G$ is injective.

concepts.c:group-action: The action on $\Omega$ detects nontrivial elements.
concepts.c:free-product: The free product is the source group, and its elements are reduced words.
concepts.c:reduced-word: A reduced word is the normal form of an element of the free product.

statement: Assume Zorn's lemma. Let $L$ be a [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) with least element $0$ and greatest element $1$. Every [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of $L$ with $1 \notin I$ lies in a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $P$, an ideal with $1 \notin P$ such that $a \wedge b \in P$ implies $a \in P$ or $b \in P$.

hypotheses.text: $L$ is a [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) with least element $0$ and greatest element $1$.
$I$ is an [ideal](c:ideal) of $L$ (a down-closed set closed under joins) with $1 \notin I$.

conclusion: There is a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $P$ of $L$ with $I \subseteq P$.

proofs.name: A maximal proper ideal is prime
proofs.slogan: Take an ideal that is maximal among proper ideals above $I$, and show with distributivity that it is prime.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Zorn's lemma is stronger than needed, because the theorem follows from the ultrafilter principle.

roles.why: The ideal $I$ starts the family, and $1 \notin I$ keeps all members proper.
Distributivity gives $(r \vee a) \wedge (r \vee b) = r \vee (a \wedge b)$, and $1$ is the top element.

steps.slogan: Collect the ideals that contain $I$ and omit $1$ into a family $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of ideals $J$ of $L$ with $I \subseteq J$ and $1 \notin J$, ordered by inclusion. It contains $I$, so it is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Show that every nonempty [chain](c:chain) in $\mathcal P$ has an upper bound in $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: Let $U$ be the union of a nonempty chain. Two elements of $U$ lie in one member, so their join lies in that member and in $U$. The set $U$ is down-closed, and $1 \notin U$ since every member omits $1$. So $U \in \mathcal P$.

steps.slogan: Extract a maximal element $P$ of $\mathcal P$ by Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: The family $\mathcal P$ is nonempty and every chain has an upper bound. Zorn's lemma gives an ideal $P \supseteq I$ with $1 \notin P$ such that no larger ideal omits $1$.

steps.slogan: Show that for $a \notin P$ some $p \in P$ has $p \vee a = 1$.
steps.detail: The set $P_a = \{x : x \le p \vee a \text{ for some } p \in P\}$ is an ideal that contains $P$ and $a$. It is larger than $P$, so $P_a \notin \mathcal P$ by maximality. So $1 \in P_a$, that is, $1 \le p \vee a$ for some $p \in P$.

steps.slogan: Use distributivity to show that $a \wedge b \in P$ forces $a \in P$ or $b \in P$.
steps.detail: Suppose $a \wedge b \in P$ but $a, b \notin P$. Step 4 gives $p, q \in P$ with $p \vee a = 1 = q \vee b$. Put $r = p \vee q \in P$, so $r \vee a = 1 = r \vee b$. Then $1 = (r \vee a) \wedge (r \vee b) = r \vee (a \wedge b) \in P$, a contradiction.

concepts.c:distributive-lattice: Distributivity is the property that makes a maximal ideal prime.
concepts.c:ideal: The family consists of ideals, and the ideal $I$ is the starting point.
concepts.c:prime-ideal: The maximal ideal of the family is the prime ideal that we need.
concepts.c:chain: A union of a chain of ideals is the upper bound.

source.note: Standard Zorn argument; see Davey and Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order (2nd ed.), on the prime ideal theorem.

statement: Every finite [separable](c:is-separable) [field extension](c:field-extension) $E/F$ is simple: there is $\alpha \in E$ with $E = F(\alpha)$.

hypotheses.text: $E/F$ is a finite [field extension](c:field-extension): $E$ has finite dimension over $F$.
$E/F$ is [separable](c:is-separable): every element of $E$ has a separable minimal polynomial over $F$.

conclusion: There is an element $\alpha \in E$ with $E = F(\alpha)$.

proofs.name: Avoid the bad scalars
proofs.slogan: Take a generator of the cyclic unit group for finite $F$, and for infinite $F$ merge two generators with a well-chosen scalar.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A finite base field uses a cyclic group, and an infinite one uses the gcd argument for two generators.

roles.why: Finite dimension gives finitely many generators for $E$, and a finite $E$ when $F$ is finite.
Separability makes the roots of $g$ simple, so the gcd is linear.

steps.slogan: If $F$ is finite, take a generator $\alpha$ of the cyclic group $E^{\times}$.
steps.detail: Then $E$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field), and its multiplicative group is a [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) generated by some $\alpha$. Every nonzero element is a power of $\alpha$, so $F(\alpha) = E$.

steps.slogan: If $F$ is infinite, choose a scalar $c$ outside a finite bad set and put $\gamma = \alpha + c\beta$.
steps.detail: Let $f, g$ be the minimal polynomials of $\alpha, \beta$, with roots $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_j$ in a splitting field. The scalars $c = -(\alpha_i - \alpha)/(\beta_j - \beta)$ with $\beta_j \ne \beta$ are finitely many. Choose $c \in F$ outside them.

steps.slogan: Show that $\beta \in F(\gamma)$ with a gcd of two polynomials over $F(\gamma)$.
steps.detail: Over $K = F(\gamma)$ let $h = \gcd\big(g(X),\, f(\gamma - cX)\big)$. It has the root $\beta$. By the choice of $c$ no other root of $g$ is a root of $f(\gamma - cX)$, and $g$ has simple roots, so $h$ is linear: $h = X - \beta$ up to a unit. Its coefficients lie in $K$, so $\beta \in K$ and $\alpha = \gamma - c\beta \in K$.

steps.slogan: Adjoin the generators of $E$ one at a time and merge each into one element.
steps.detail: Since $\dim_F E < \infty$, we have $E = F(e_1, \dots, e_r)$. If $F(e_1, \dots, e_s) = F(\alpha)$, the previous step gives $\gamma$ with $F(\alpha, e_{s+1}) = F(\gamma)$, since $e_{s+1}$ is separable. After $r$ steps, $E = F(\gamma)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the finite and the infinite case to give a primitive element of $E/F$.
steps.detail: If $F$ is finite, step 1 gives $\alpha$ with $E = F(\alpha)$. If $F$ is infinite, step 4 gives $\gamma$ with $E = F(\gamma)$. In both cases $E/F$ is simple.

concepts.c:field-extension: The theorem describes the structure of a finite extension.
concepts.c:is-separable: Separability makes the gcd of the two polynomials linear.
concepts.c:finite-field: A finite base field makes $E$ a finite field, with a cyclic unit group.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: A generator of the cyclic unit group is the primitive element.

source.note: mathlib splits on finiteness of $F$: exists_primitive_element_of_finite_bot (IsCyclic unit group) and primitive_element_inf_aux with induction_on_adjoin.

proofs.name: Finitely many intermediate fields
proofs.slogan: A finite separable extension has finitely many intermediate fields, so two scalars give the same field $F(\alpha + c\beta)$, and that field holds both generators.
proofs.scope: Infinite $F$ by the counting argument; finite $F$ by the cyclic unit group. Both cases give the whole theorem.

roles.why: Finite degree gives a finite Galois closure and finitely many generators.
Separability makes the normal closure a Galois extension.

steps.slogan: Embed $E$ in a finite Galois extension $L$ of $F$.
steps.detail: Let $L$ be the splitting field over $E$ of the minimal polynomials over $F$ of a basis of $E$. These polynomials are separable, so $L/F$ is finite and Galois.

steps.slogan: Show that $E/F$ has only finitely many intermediate fields.
steps.detail: The group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)$ is finite, so it has finitely many subgroups. By the Galois correspondence $L/F$ has finitely many [intermediate fields](c:intermediate-field), and so does the subextension $E/F$.

steps.slogan: Map each scalar $c \in F$ to the field $F(\alpha + c\beta)$ and find two scalars with the same image.
steps.detail: Let $F$ be infinite and $\alpha, \beta \in E$. Infinitely many scalars map to finitely many fields, so $F(\alpha + c\beta) = F(\alpha + c'\beta) =: K$ for some $c \ne c'$.

steps.slogan: Show that $K$ contains $\alpha$ and $\beta$, so $F(\alpha, \beta) = F(\alpha + c\beta)$.
steps.detail: Both $\alpha + c\beta$ and $\alpha + c'\beta$ lie in $K$, so $(c - c')\beta \in K$. Since $c - c' \in F^{\times}$, we get $\beta \in K$ and then $\alpha \in K$. So $F(\alpha, \beta) \subseteq K \subseteq F(\alpha, \beta)$.

steps.slogan: Merge the generators of $E$ two at a time, and treat finite $F$ by its cyclic unit group.
steps.detail: For infinite $F$, write $E = F(e_1, \dots, e_r)$ and apply the previous step again and again. For finite $F$, the [finite field](c:finite-field) $E$ has a cyclic unit group with a generator $\alpha$, so $E = F(\alpha)$.

concepts.c:field-extension: The theorem describes the structure of a finite extension.
concepts.c:is-separable: Separability makes the closure Galois, so intermediate fields are finite in number.
concepts.c:intermediate-field: Finiteness of the set of intermediate fields drives the counting argument.
concepts.c:finite-field: A finite base field makes $E$ a finite field, with a cyclic unit group.

source.note: Artin's argument; see S. Lang, Algebra, Chapter V, Theorem 4.6. Mathlib has this route as exists_primitive_element_of_finite_intermediateField.

statement: Let $q(x) = x^{T}Ax$ be a real [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $A$ [symmetric](c:symmetric-matrix). There are an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) $u_1, \dots, u_n$ and reals $\lambda_i$ with $A u_i = \lambda_i u_i$ and $q(\sum y_i u_i) = \sum \lambda_i y_i^2$. The basis can be chosen positively oriented.

hypotheses.text: The function $q(x) = x^{T}Ax$ is a real [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The matrix $A$ is real and [symmetric](c:symmetric-matrix).

conclusion: A positively oriented [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) of eigenvectors $u_i$ puts $q$ in the diagonal form $\sum \lambda_i y_i^2$, where $\lambda_i$ are the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of $A$.

proofs.name: Spectral theorem
proofs.slogan: Diagonalize the symmetric matrix of the form with an orthonormal eigenbasis, then substitute the new coordinates.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $n = 0$ and repeated eigenvalues, where the axes are not unique. A sign flip makes the basis positively oriented.

roles.why: Symmetry lets the spectral theorem give an orthonormal eigenbasis.
The value $q(x) = x^{T}Ax$ is what the substitution diagonalizes.

steps.slogan: Obtain an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A$ from the spectral theorem.
steps.detail: The spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices gives an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) $u_1, \dots, u_n$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $Au_i = \lambda_i u_i$ and every $\lambda_i$ real.

steps.slogan: Substitute $x = \sum y_i u_i$ into the form.
steps.detail: Let $Q$ be the orthogonal matrix with columns $u_i$, so $x = Qy$. Since $Au_j = \lambda_j u_j$ and $u_i^{T}u_j = \delta_{ij}$, we get $Q^{T}AQ = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)$. So $q(x) = y^{T}Q^{T}AQy = \sum \lambda_i y_i^2$.

steps.slogan: Flip the sign of one axis to make the change of variables a rotation.
steps.detail: The orthogonal matrix $Q$ has $\det Q = \pm 1$. If $\det Q = -1$, replace $u_1$ by $-u_1$, which is still a unit eigenvector. This changes $y_1$ to $-y_1$, so $\lambda_1 y_1^2$ is unchanged, and now $\det Q = 1$.

concepts.c:symmetric-matrix: A symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: The eigenbasis gives the perpendicular principal axes.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The eigenvalues are the diagonal coefficients of the form.

source.note: The spectral theorem applied to a quadratic form; see G. Strang, Linear Algebra and Its Applications, section on the principal axis theorem.

proofs.name: Maximize on the sphere
proofs.slogan: Maximize the form on the unit sphere to find one axis, then repeat on the orthogonal complement.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by induction on $n$. The case $n = 0$ is empty, and a sign flip gives the positive orientation.

roles.why: The continuous function $q$ has a maximum on the compact sphere.
Symmetry makes $v^{T}Au$ the derivative of $q$ and keeps $u_1^{\perp}$ invariant.

steps.slogan: Choose a point $u_1$ of the unit sphere where $q$ is largest.
steps.detail: The unit sphere is compact and $q$ is continuous, so the extreme value theorem gives a maximizer $u_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the maximizer $u_1$ is an [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) of $A$.
steps.detail: For $v \perp u_1$ and small $t$, the unit vector $(u_1 + tv)/\sqrt{1 + t^2|v|^2}$ gives $q(u_1) + 2t\,v^{T}Au_1 + O(t^2) \le q(u_1)$. This holds for both signs of $t$, so $v^{T}Au_1 = 0$. Hence $Au_1 = \lambda_1 u_1$ with $\lambda_1 = q(u_1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the orthogonal complement $u_1^{\perp}$ is invariant under $A$.
steps.detail: For $v \perp u_1$, symmetry gives $u_1^{T}Av = (Au_1)^{T}v = \lambda_1 u_1^{T}v = 0$. So $Av \in u_1^{\perp}$, and $A$ restricts to a symmetric map of $u_1^{\perp}$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the argument on $u_1^{\perp}$ to complete the orthonormal basis.
steps.detail: The space $u_1^{\perp}$ has dimension $n - 1$ and $A$ is symmetric on it. By induction it has an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) $u_2, \dots, u_n$ of eigenvectors. With $u_1$ this is an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

steps.slogan: Read off the diagonal form of $q$ in the basis $u_i$.
steps.detail: For $x = \sum y_i u_i$ we get $q(x) = \sum_{i,j} y_i y_j u_i^{T}Au_j = \sum \lambda_i y_i^2$. If the basis is negatively oriented, replacing $u_1$ by $-u_1$ keeps this form and makes it positive.

concepts.c:quadratic-form: The theorem diagonalizes this form, and the proof maximizes it.
concepts.c:symmetric-matrix: Symmetry makes the maximizer an eigenvector and keeps the complement invariant.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: The repeated maximizers form the orthonormal basis of principal axes.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The maximal value $q(u_1)$ is the first eigenvalue.
concepts.c:eigenvector: A maximizer of the form on the sphere is an eigenvector.

source.note: The maximization proof of the spectral theorem; see P. D. Lax, Linear Algebra and Its Applications, chapter on self-adjoint mappings.
